pos: n. pl. (birds of costly plumage imported by Solomon's fleet; in Job, a creature given splendour without wisdom)
etymology: Old English pawa, from Latin pavo, + cock. The Hebrew of Kings is tukkiyyim, a loanword from the far trade routes; the word in Job 39 is a different term, of the wing that displays and cannot save.
biblical_def: Peacocks come into Scripture twice, and for opposite reasons. In the trade lists they are the last item of Solomon's luxury: “once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” (1Ki 10:22; and again 2Ch 9:21). In Job they are an argument. The LORD asks, “Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich?” (Job 39:13), and then explains why the question stings: “God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding” (Job 39:17). Magnificent plumage and no sense — and God made her so on purpose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the peacock as a large and beautiful fowl of the genus Pavo, remarkable for the splendor of its plumage and the train it can erect and expand.
webster_full: PEACOCK, n. A large and beautiful fowl of the genus Pavo, a native of India, remarkable for the beauty of its plumage and the length of its train, which it erects and expands.
PLUMAGE, n. The feathers that cover a fowl.
scriptures: For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: every three years once came the ships of Tarshish bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich?
Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding.
corruption_summary: God points to a splendid, foolish bird as evidence of His freedom, and the same chapter that gives the feathers withholds the understanding.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 39 is the LORD's catalogue of creatures man neither made nor manages, and the ostrich passage is the sharpest of them. She is given goodly wings and denied wisdom; she leaves her eggs in the dust and forgets that a foot may crush them; and the reason offered is not evolutionary advantage but divine decision — God hath deprived her. Splendour and folly in the same animal, by design, so that Job may learn that the Creator is under no obligation to distribute His gifts by any scheme man would recognize as fair. This is the doctrine of divine freedom, taught by a bird.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that beauty is not merit and gifts are not wisdom. Solomon's peacocks arrived on the same ships as the gold, in the reign whose end was idolatry; the display outlasted the discernment. Scripture is steady on this — favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD shall be praised. The temptation the peacock rebukes is the reflex that reads the gift as a verdict on the person, and it runs in both directions: it flatters the splendid and despises the plain, and it is wrong both times.
roots_summary: Hebrew tukkiyyim (H8500), peacocks of the trade fleets; renanim (H7443), the crying bird of Job 39; chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew tukkiyyim (H8500) — peacocks; 1 Kings 10:22, 2 Chronicles 9:21 only.
Hebrew renanim (H7443) — the peacock or ostrich of Job 39:13.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; Job 39:17, Proverbs 1:7, 9:10.
Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, discernment; Job 39:17, Proverbs 4:7.
Hebrew shenhabbim (H8143) — ivory; 1 Kings 10:22, 2 Chronicles 9:21.
usage: “Gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” — the last item of Solomon's luxury.
“Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks?” — the LORD's question out of the whirlwind.
“God hath deprived her of wisdom” — splendour and folly in one creature, by design.

pos: n. pl. (exotic animals brought home by the fleets of Solomon; a mark of imperial luxury)
etymology: Old English apa. The Hebrew qoph is a loanword travelling with the animal itself along the trade routes to Tarshish, appearing in Scripture only in the two parallel accounts of Solomon's navy.
biblical_def: Apes appear in the Bible exactly twice, both times in an inventory. “For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” (1Ki 10:22), and Chronicles repeats it of Huram's ships (2Ch 9:21). They are the tail end of a list that begins with bullion and ends with curiosities — a king so rich that novelty had become a category of import. The whole chapter runs to excess, and the chapter after it in Kings records what the wealth and the wives together did to Solomon's heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ape as a genus of quadrumanous animals without a tail, and figuratively one who imitates another servilely.
webster_full: APE, n. A genus of quadrumanous animals, the character of which is, that they have no tails. In common use, the word extends to monkeys of all sorts.
APE, n. One who imitates servilely, in allusion to the manners of the ape; a silly fellow.
APE, v.t. To imitate servilely; to mimick, as an ape imitates human actions.
scriptures: For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: every three years once came the ships of Tarshish bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
Job 9:10
Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number.

Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth.
corruption_summary: Solomon's apes are a footnote to a reign that gained the world and lost its heart, and Deuteronomy had forbidden the multiplying beforehand.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 17 legislated for a king before Israel had one: he shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to multiply horses; neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away; neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold. First Kings 10 and 11 read like a deliberate audit against that statute. Horses out of Egypt, silver as stones in Jerusalem, seven hundred wives, and three-year voyages bringing apes and peacocks — and then the sentence: his wives turned away his heart. The apes are not the sin; they are the receipt.

The corruption to name is the assumption that prosperity vindicates. Solomon's reign is the strongest case in Scripture for the opposite reading — that God may grant a man everything he asked and everything he did not, and the man may still end his life building high places for Chemosh and Molech. The prosperity teaching that reads wealth as evidence of divine approval has to skip 1 Kings 11 entirely to survive, and so does its secular cousin, which reads success as evidence of virtue. Scripture files the apes under warning.
roots_summary: Hebrew qoph (H6971), ape; Tarshish (H8659), the far trading port; oni (H590), a fleet of ships.
roots_lines: Hebrew qoph (H6971) — ape; 1 Kings 10:22, 2 Chronicles 9:21 only.
Hebrew Tarshish (H8659) — Tarshish, a distant port; 1 Kings 10:22, Jonah 1:3, Isaiah 23:1.
Hebrew oni (H590) — ships, a fleet; 1 Kings 10:22, Isaiah 33:21.
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply, increase; Deuteronomy 17:16, 17:17.
Hebrew natah (H5186) — to turn aside, incline; 1 Kings 11:3, 11:4.
usage: “Bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” — the fleet's three-year manifest.
“Every three years once came the ships of Tarshish” — Chronicles' parallel record.
An inventory of curiosities from a reign that ended in high places.

pos: n. pl. (turtledoves; the poor man's offering appointed in the law; Hebrew tor)
etymology: Latin turtur, an imitation of the bird's call. In the KJV turtle is always the turtledove and never the reptile — the modern sense of the word had not yet displaced the older one.
biblical_def: Turtles in Scripture are the mercy clause of the sacrificial law. Where a lamb was beyond a family's means, the LORD appointed birds: “on the eighth day she shall take unto her two turtles, or two young pigeons, and bring them unto the priest” (Lev 15:29); so also for the Nazarite's defilement, “on the eighth day he shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons, to the priest” (Num 6:10), and for the man who could not bring a lamb, “two turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Lev 15:14). The provision matters at the end of the story as well: Mary's offering at the temple was the pair of birds, which is Luke's quiet way of telling us the household Christ was born into.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the turtle as the turtledove, a species of pigeon proverbial for its plaintive note and the constancy of its mate.
webster_full: TURTLE, n. The turtle-dove, a species of pigeon, remarkable for the plaintiveness of its note and for the constancy of the pair.
TURTLEDOVE, n. A species of dove, noted for its affection to its mate.
scriptures: And on the eighth day she shall take unto her two turtles, or two young pigeons, and bring them unto the priest, to the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.
Num 6:10
And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons, to the priest, to the door of the tabernacle of the congregation:
And on the eighth day he shall take to him two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, and come before the LORD unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, and give them unto the priest:
Son 1:15
Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves' eyes.
corruption_summary: The law made a way for the poor to come without lowering what atonement required, and the incarnate Son was redeemed with the poor man's birds.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus does not offer the poor a discount on holiness; it offers them a substitute they can carry. The blood is still shed, the priest still makes atonement, the sin is still covered — and the family that cannot reach a lamb brings two birds and goes home clean. That is the shape of grace in the ceremonial law: God will be approached on His terms, and God Himself supplies terms the poorest household can meet. Luke 2 turns the provision into a fact about Christ. Mary offered the birds, which is to say the Lord of glory entered the world in a family that could not afford the lamb, having come to be the Lamb.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that access and standard are not enemies. Two errors stand opposite each other here, and the turtledove refutes both. The first says that God's requirements must be softened for the weak, and so quietly abolishes atonement in the name of kindness. The second says that the poor must climb to the rich man's offering, and so bars the door God opened. Leviticus does neither. It holds the standard exactly and provides for the poor exactly, which is what the cross does in full.
roots_summary: Hebrew tor (H8449), turtledove; yonah (H3123), pigeon or dove; kaphar (H3722), to cover, make atonement.
roots_lines: Hebrew tor (H8449) — turtledove; Leviticus 15:29, Numbers 6:10, Genesis 15:9.
Hebrew yonah (H3123) — dove, pigeon; Leviticus 15:14, Genesis 8:8, Song of Solomon 2:14.
Hebrew kaphar (H3722) — to cover, atone; Leviticus 12:8, 16:30.
Hebrew chattath (H2403) — sin, sin offering; Leviticus 15:30, Numbers 6:11.
Greek trugon (G5167) — turtledove; Luke 2:24 only.
usage: “Two turtles, or two young pigeons” — the poor man's appointed offering.
“On the eighth day he shall bring two turtles” — the Nazarite's cleansing.
The birds Mary brought — Luke's note on the household of the incarnate Son.

pos: n. pl. (in Scripture almost always a figure of pursuing enemies; and once, the sweetness found in the carcase of a lion)
etymology: Old English beo. Hebrew deborah, from a root of ordering or speaking — the same word that names the prophetess who judged Israel under her palm tree.
biblical_def: Bees in the Bible chase. Moses reminds the generation that would not go up, “the Amorites, which dwelt in that mountain, came out against you, and chased you, as bees do, and destroyed you in Seir” (Deu 1:44). The psalmist knows the same terror and the same deliverance: “They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns: for in the name of the LORD I will destroy them” (Psa 118:12). The exception is Samson's riddle: “there was a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion” (Jdg 14:8), out of which he framed it — “Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Jdg 14:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the bee as an insect of the genus Apis, of which the honey-bee is the most useful, living in swarms or societies and remarkable for its industry.
webster_full: BEE, n. An insect of the genus Apis. The honey-bee lives in swarms or societies, of from 10,000 to 50,000 individuals, and is remarkable for its industry and the regularity of its work.
SWARM, n. A large number or body of small animals or insects, particularly when in motion; especially a great number of bees which emigrate from a hive at once.
scriptures: Deu 1:44
And the Amorites, which dwelt in that mountain, came out against you, and chased you, as bees do, and destroyed you in Seir, even unto Hormah.
They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns: for in the name of the LORD I will destroy them.
Jdg 14:8
And after a time he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcase of the lion: and, behold, there was a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion.
And he said unto them, Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle.
corruption_summary: Samson's riddle is true of God's providence and false as Samson used it, since he got his sweetness by handling what the law called unclean.
corruption_paragraphs: Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. As a statement about God's way in the world the riddle is exact — Joseph's brothers meant it for evil and God meant it for good; the cross is the murder of the Son turned into the salvation of the world. But Judges is not commending Samson. A Nazarite had touched a carcase, taken honey out of it, and fed it to his parents without telling them what it was; the riddle is built on his own defilement, and the marriage it decorates was contracted against the law. God brought good out of that too, which is the doctrine of providence and never an excuse for the deed.

The corruption to name is the misuse of Romans 8:28 as a permission rather than a comfort. That God works all things together for good to them that love Him is a promise given to sufferers, not a licence given to sinners, and Paul anticipated the abuse in the next chapter but one: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. Samson is the standing case study. His life ends in the temple of Dagon with his eyes out, and the epistle to the Hebrews still lists him among the faithful — both facts are in the text, and neither cancels the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew deborah (H1682), bee; debash (H1706), honey; chidah (H2420), a riddle or dark saying.
roots_lines: Hebrew deborah (H1682) — bee; Deuteronomy 1:44, Judges 14:8, Psalm 118:12, Isaiah 7:18.
Hebrew debash (H1706) — honey; Judges 14:8, Exodus 3:8, Psalm 19:10.
Hebrew chidah (H2420) — riddle, dark saying; Judges 14:14, Proverbs 1:6.
Hebrew sabab (H5437) — to compass, surround; Psalm 118:12, Joshua 6:3.
Hebrew nebelah (H5038) — carcase, dead body; Leviticus 11:39, Judges 14:8.
usage: “Chased you, as bees do” — Moses on the defeat at Hormah.
“They compassed me about like bees” — and were quenched as the fire of thorns.
“Out of the strong came forth sweetness” — Samson's riddle, and its defilement.

pos: n. (a constellation named in Job and Amos as a work of God's hand; Hebrew kesil)
etymology: Greek Orion, the hunter of the myths. The Hebrew kesil means the fool or the strong one bound — a giant fixed in the sky, and the Scripture speaks of loosing or binding his bands.
biblical_def: Job names Orion among God's ordinary works: “Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south” (Job 9:9). Out of the whirlwind the LORD turns it into a question Job cannot answer: “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31). Amos preaches it to a nation about to fall: “Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning… The LORD is his name” (Amo 5:8). Isaiah presses the same claim on the exiles: “he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might” (Isa 40:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Orion as a constellation in the southern hemisphere, containing seventy-eight stars, mentioned in the book of Job.
webster_full: ORION, n. A constellation in the southern hemisphere, containing seventy eight stars. Job ix. 9.
CONSTELLATION, n. A cluster of fixed stars; an assemblage of several stars comprehended within some assumed figure.
scriptures: Job 9:9
Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.
Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
Amo 5:8

Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name:

Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth.
corruption_summary: Scripture uses the constellation names of the nations and empties them of divinity, naming the stars while denying that the stars rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The neighbours of Israel worshipped the constellations; Job and Amos name them and hand them to their Maker. This is the Bible's standing method with pagan material — not to invent a rival vocabulary, but to take the ordinary names of the sky and put a Creator behind them. Amos does it in a sentence of judgment: seek Him that maketh the seven stars and Orion. Isaiah does it by bringing out the host by number and calling them all by names. The stars are counted, named, commanded, and none of them fails, which is exactly why none of them may be feared.

The corruption to name is astrology, ancient and modern. Deuteronomy 4 forbids lifting up the eyes to the sun, moon and stars and being driven to worship them; Isaiah 47 mocks the astrologers and the monthly prognosticators and tells Babylon to let them save her if they can; Jeremiah 10 says be not dismayed at the signs of heaven, for the heathen are dismayed at them. The horoscope survives in the modern West as a harmless amusement precisely because nobody believes it enough to be judged for it, which is its own indictment — a divination too trivial to obey and too flattering to abandon. Orion has no influence. Orion has a Maker.
roots_summary: Hebrew kesil (H3685), Orion, the bound giant; kimah (H3598), the Pleiades; ash / ayish (H5906), Arcturus and his sons.
roots_lines: Hebrew kesil (H3685) — Orion; Job 9:9, 38:31, Amos 5:8, Isaiah 13:10.
Hebrew kimah (H3598) — the Pleiades, seven stars; Job 9:9, 38:31, Amos 5:8.
Hebrew moshekah (H4189) — bands, cords; Job 38:31.
Hebrew tsaba (H6635) — host, army; Isaiah 40:26, Genesis 2:1.
Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — shadow of death; Amos 5:8, Psalm 23:4.
usage: “Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” — Job's catalogue of ordinary works.
“Canst thou… loose the bands of Orion?” — the LORD out of the whirlwind.
“Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion” — Amos to a falling nation.

pos: n. (a star or constellation of the northern sky, named twice in Job; Hebrew ash, ayish)
etymology: Greek Arktouros, the bear-watcher. The KJV uses it for Hebrew ash and ayish, spoken of in Job 38 as having “sons” — a group of stars guided together as a company.
biblical_def: Arcturus stands in both of Job's star-lists. In the first, Job himself confesses the LORD as the one “which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south” (Job 9:9), adding that He “doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number” (Job 9:10). In the second, the LORD turns Job's own confession into an examination: “Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” (Job 38:32), and immediately after, “Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?” (Job 38:33). The stars are governed, and Job is not the governor.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Arcturus as a fixed star of the first magnitude in the constellation Bootes, whose name signifies the bear-keeper.
webster_full: ARCTURUS, n. A fixed star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Bootes. Its name signifies the bear-keeper, from its situation behind the tail of the great bear.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
scriptures: Job 9:9
Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.
Job 9:10
Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number.
Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?
Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?
corruption_summary: The whirlwind speech answers Job's suffering with astronomy, and the answer is a Person rather than an explanation.
corruption_paragraphs: Job asked why. God answered with the sea, the snow, the stars, the wild goats and the war horse, and never once addressed the question directly. That is not evasion; it is the deepest possible answer. Job's trouble was that he could not see a government behind his pain, and God's reply was to walk him through a universe of governed things — Mazzaroth brought forth in his season, Arcturus guided with his sons, the ordinances of heaven set and kept. If the constellations are led about like a flock, the sufferer is not adrift. Job's repentance in chapter 42 is not the discovery of a reason but the sight of a Ruler.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the biblical answer to affliction is the character and government of God rather than an account of causes. Two failures crowd in on this. One demands the reason and will not worship without it, which is Job's error before chapter 42. The other invents reasons on God's behalf and hands them to sufferers, which is the error of Job's friends, whom God rebuked. The book ends with the friends needing Job's prayer, and with Job saying he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear but now his eye seeth Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew ash / ayish (H5906), Arcturus with his sons; mazzaroth (H4216), the constellations of the zodiac in their seasons; chuqqah (H2708), ordinance, statute.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayish (H5906) — Arcturus, the Bear with her sons; Job 9:9, 38:32.
Hebrew mazzaroth (H4216) — the constellations in their seasons; Job 38:32 only.
Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — ordinance, appointed statute; Job 38:33, Jeremiah 31:35.
Hebrew mishtar (H4896) — dominion, rule; Job 38:33 only.
Hebrew nachah (H5148) — to lead, guide; Job 38:32, Psalm 23:3.
usage: “Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” — Job's own confession.
“Canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” — the confession turned into a question.
“Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven?” — the government Job could not see.

pos: n. (frozen water; in Job and the Psalms a witness to the power and the ease of God; Hebrew qerach)
etymology: Old English is. Hebrew qerach covers ice, frost, and crystal; the same root stands behind the terrible crystal stretched over the heads of the living creatures in Ezekiel 1.
biblical_def: Ice enters Scripture as an argument for God's power in small things. The LORD asks Job, “Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?” (Job 38:29). Elihu had already said how it is made: “By the breath of God frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened” (Job 37:10). The psalmist marvels at the ease of it: “He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?” (Psa 147:17), having just said, “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes” (Psa 147:16). Job's friends had also seen the treacherous side, brooks “blackish by reason of the ice” that vanish when they are wanted (Job 6:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ice as water or other fluid congealed, a solid transparent body formed by the congelation of a fluid by means of cold.
webster_full: ICE, n. Water or other fluid congealed, or in a solid state; a solid, transparent, brittle body, formed by the congelation of a fluid, by means of the abstraction of heat.
CONGEAL, v.t. To change from a fluid to a solid state, as by cold; to freeze.
HOARFROST, n. The white particles of ice formed by the congelation of dew or watery vapors.
scriptures: Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?
By the breath of God frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened.
He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.
He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?
corruption_summary: Scripture treats weather as the direct working of God, and says so in the same breath in which it treats it as ordinary.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 147 has no category for a natural process that runs itself. God giveth the snow, scattereth the hoarfrost, casteth forth the ice, sendeth out His word and melteth them, causeth His wind to blow and the waters flow. This is not a denial of second causes — the Reformed confessions have always affirmed that God ordinarily works through means, and Job 37 is full of the mechanics of cloud and vapour. It is a denial that the means are a substitute for the Agent. The ice has a Maker in the same sense the world has, and the psalm expects the reader to feel the cold and think of Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a full account of the mechanism is not a rival to the doctrine of providence. Deism made the two compete — a God who wound the world and withdrew — and practical deism is still the working theology of many who confess better on paper: God is invoked for the extraordinary and assumed absent from the ordinary. Job 38 will not divide the world that way. The same voice that made Behemoth asks who fathered the frost, and the answer to both is one.
roots_summary: Hebrew qerach (H7140), ice, frost, crystal; kephowr (H3713), hoarfrost; ruach (H7307), breath, wind, Spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew qerach (H7140) — ice, frost; Job 6:16, 38:29, Psalm 147:17.
Hebrew kephowr (H3713) — hoarfrost; Job 38:29, Psalm 147:16, Exodus 16:14.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — breath, wind, spirit; Job 37:10, Genesis 1:2.
Hebrew yatsaq / shalak (H7993) — to cast forth; Psalm 147:17.
Hebrew qarah (H7135) — cold; Psalm 147:17, Proverbs 25:20.
usage: “Out of whose womb came the ice?” — the LORD's question to Job.
“By the breath of God frost is given” — Elihu on the mechanics of winter.
“He casteth forth his ice like morsels” — power exercised as easily as crumbs.

pos: n. (vapour; in Genesis the watering of the first earth, in the New Testament a figure of blindness and of judgment)
etymology: Old English mist. Hebrew ed, a vapour or flow; the Greek achlus of Acts 13 is a dimness that falls over the eye, and the zophos of 2 Peter is the blackness of settled gloom.
biblical_def: Before the rain there was a mist: “there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground” (Gen 2:6). In Acts the word turns dark. Paul withstands Elymas the sorcerer — “thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand” (Act 13:11). Peter uses it of false teachers: “These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever” (2Pe 2:17). James takes the vapour and turns it on the reader: “what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jas 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mist as water falling in very numerous but fine and almost imperceptible drops, and figuratively that which dims or darkens the understanding.
webster_full: MIST, n. Water falling in very numerous, but fine and almost imperceptible drops. Also, a low thin fog.
MIST, n. That which dims or darkens, and causes error or obscurity in the understanding.
MIST, v.t. To cloud; to cover with vapor.
scriptures: Gen 2:6
But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground.

And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand.
These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.
Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: Peter and Jude describe false teachers as wells without water and clouds without rain — the promise of refreshment with nothing in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Peter 2 is one of the most concentrated passages on false teaching in Scripture, and its images are all about emptiness dressed as supply. Wells without water. Clouds carried with a tempest. Great swelling words of vanity. They promise liberty and are themselves the servants of corruption. The judgment matches the crime exactly: to men who traded in fog, the mist of darkness is reserved for ever. Elymas in Acts 13 receives the same sentence in miniature and in time — the man who sought to turn the deputy from the faith is led about by the hand, seeking someone to guide him.

The corruption to name is the confusion of impressiveness with substance. Peter's false teachers are not obviously shabby; they are eloquent, confident, and popular, and many shall follow their pernicious ways. The test he gives is not style but water — does the well have any? Does the cloud carry rain? A ministry is to be judged by whether the hearers are fed on the doctrine of God, forgiven through the blood of Christ, and made holy by the Spirit, and no amount of atmosphere substitutes. James adds the personal edge: the hearer's own life is a vapour, so the question of who is feeding him is not academic.
roots_summary: Hebrew ed (H108), mist, vapour; Greek achlus (G887), a dimness over the eyes; Greek zophos (G2217), the blackness of darkness.
roots_lines: Hebrew ed (H108) — mist, vapour; Genesis 2:6, Job 36:27.
Greek achlus (G887) — mist, dimness; Acts 13:11 only.
Greek zophos (G2217) — blackness, gloom; 2 Peter 2:17, Jude 1:13.
Greek atmis (G822) — vapour; James 4:14, Acts 2:19.
Greek homichle (G3658) — a mist or fog; 2 Peter 2:17.
usage: “There went up a mist from the earth” — the watering of the first ground.
“There fell on him a mist and a darkness” — the sorcerer led about by the hand.
“Wells without water” — Peter's verdict on false teachers.

pos: n. pl. (the divided hoof of a clean beast; the talons of a bird; the nails of a man under judgment)
etymology: Old English clawu. The KJV uses the word for the cloven hoof of Deuteronomy 14, for birds' talons, and for the nails Nebuchadnezzar grew in his madness — the mark, in every case, of what a creature is.
biblical_def: The law used claws to mark the clean: “every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6) — the same rule Leviticus states as “whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud” (Lev 11:3). Daniel uses them to mark a man unmade: Nebuchadnezzar “was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen… till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws” (Dan 4:33). Zechariah uses them to mark a shepherd who devours his own flock: “he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces” (Zec 11:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a claw as the sharp hooked nail of a beast or bird, and in another sense the whole foot of an animal armed with hooked nails.
webster_full: CLAW, n. The sharp hooked nail of a quadruped, bird or other animal.
CLAW, n. The whole foot of an animal armed with hooked nails.
CLOVENFOOTED, a. Having the foot divided into two parts, as an ox.
scriptures: Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.
Dan 4:33

The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws.

For, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, which shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken, nor feed that that standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces.
Dan 7:19

Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast, which was diverse from all the others, exceeding dreadful, whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet;
corruption_summary: The king who said, is not this great Babylon that I have built, was given the nails of a bird and put out to grass until he knew who reigns.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 4 is the fullest treatment in Scripture of what pride does to a man and what God does to pride. Nebuchadnezzar walks in his palace, says is not this great Babylon that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty, and the word is still in his mouth when the sentence falls. He is driven from men, his hair grows like feathers, his nails like birds' claws, and he eats grass as oxen until he knows that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men. The restoration is as remarkable as the judgment: he lifts up his eyes to heaven, his understanding returns, and he blesses the King of heaven, all whose works are truth and His ways judgment.

The corruption to name is the doctrine that man is the measure and the maker of his own greatness. It is not a modern invention — Babel said it first, and Babylon said it best — but it is unusually well housed in a culture that speaks of building one's own truth and authoring one's own identity. Daniel 4 answers with an image rather than an argument: a man who will not acknowledge that he is a creature is given the outward form of a beast until he does. And the chapter is written in the first person, by the king, after the fact.
roots_summary: Hebrew parsah (H6541), hoof; Aramaic tephar (H2953), nail, claw; Hebrew garam (H1633), to break the bones, tear in pieces.
roots_lines: Hebrew parsah (H6541) — hoof, cloven claw; Deuteronomy 14:6, Leviticus 11:3.
Aramaic tephar (H2953) — nail, claw; Daniel 4:33, 7:19.
Hebrew garam (H1633) — to break bones, tear in pieces; Zechariah 11:16, Numbers 24:8.
Hebrew gerah (H1625) — the cud; Leviticus 11:3, Deuteronomy 14:6.
Aramaic shelet (H7981) — to rule, have dominion; Daniel 4:17, 4:25.
usage: “Cleaveth the cleft into two claws” — the law's mark of a clean beast.
“His nails like birds' claws” — a king reduced until he confessed heaven rules.
“Tear their claws in pieces” — Zechariah's worthless shepherd.

pos: n. (smell, savour; in Scripture a figure of hidden life, of settled complacency, and of revival)
etymology: Old French sentir, to feel or perceive, from Latin sentire. In Job the word is reyach, the same term used of the sweet savour of sacrifice — what rises from a thing and tells you what it is.
biblical_def: Job makes the scent of water the emblem of hope in a dead thing: “Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant” (Job 14:9) — a felled tree that smells rain and lives. Jeremiah makes it the emblem of a nation that has never been disturbed: Moab “hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed” (Jer 48:11). Hosea makes it the emblem of restoration: “they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon” (Hos 14:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scent as odor; smell; that substance which, emitted from a body, affects the olfactory organs; and also the power of smelling.
webster_full: SCENT, n. Odor; smell; that substance which, emitted from any body, affects the olfactory organs of animals.
SCENT, n. The power of smelling; the smell; as a hound of nice scent.
SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste and smell.
scriptures: Job 14:9
Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant.

Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.
Hos 14:7
They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.
Job 9:10
Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah names undisturbed ease as a judgment rather than a blessing, since Moab kept his flavour only because he was never poured out.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 48:11 is a winemaker's sentence turned into a doctrine. Wine left on its lees keeps its old taste and never improves; it must be racked from vessel to vessel to be refined. Moab had never been racked. He had been at ease from his youth, never emptied, never carried away, and the result was not maturity but a nation whose scent was not changed — the same at the end as at the beginning, and about to be broken for it. Ease is treated here as the absence of God's refining, and Scripture is consistent about it: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and if ye be without chastisement, then are ye bastards and not sons.

The corruption to name is the assumption, widespread and rarely stated, that an untroubled life is evidence of God's favour and a hard one evidence of His displeasure. Psalm 73 works through it honestly — Asaph envied the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary and understood their end. Hebrews 12 works through it doctrinally. Jeremiah 48 works through it by taking a nation that had everything the modern definition of blessing requires and calling its condition a judgment. The scent that pleases God is the one that comes off a life He has poured from vessel to vessel.
roots_summary: Hebrew reyach (H7381), scent, savour, smell; shemer (H8105), lees or dregs; chayah (H2421), to live, revive.
roots_lines: Hebrew reyach (H7381) — scent, savour; Job 14:9, Jeremiah 48:11, Genesis 8:21.
Hebrew shemer (H8105) — lees, dregs of wine; Jeremiah 48:11, Zephaniah 1:12.
Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, revive, quicken; Hosea 14:7, Psalm 119:25.
Hebrew shaanan (H7599) — to be at ease, secure; Jeremiah 48:11, Amos 6:1.
Greek osme (G3744) — odour, savour; 2 Corinthians 2:14, Philippians 4:18.
usage: “Through the scent of water it will bud” — the felled tree that smells rain.
“His scent is not changed” — Moab, never emptied from vessel to vessel.
“The scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon” — Hosea on revival.
